=== FINAL TBC – Comment Letter on PUCT Project No 58481 - Google Docs.pdf ===
​ exas Blockchain Council – Comment Letter​
T
​on PUCT Project No. 58481 (Large Load​
 ​Interconnection Standards)​
​ ia Electronic Filing​
V
​December 19, 2025​

​ ublic Utility Commission of Texas​
P
​Attn: Central Records​
 ​1701 N. Congress Avenue​
  ​Austin, Texas 78701​

​ e: Project No. 58481 – Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards (16​
R
​TAC §25.194)​

​Dear Commissioners:​

​ he Texas Blockchain Council (TBC) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the​
T
​proposed new 16 TAC §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards (Project No.​
 ​58481). TBC is an industry association representing Bitcoin mining and artificial intelligence (AI)​
  ​data center companies in Texas. Our members are among the “large load” customers that will​
   ​be directly affected by the new interconnection standards. We support the Commission’s efforts​
    ​to implement Senate Bill 6 (codified as PURA §37.0561) to accommodate large loads in a​
     ​manner that “support[s] business development in this state while minimizing the potential for​
      ​stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.” In keeping with these goals,​
       ​TBC offers the following formal comments on the proposed rule.​

​ hese targeted modifications will better align the rule with legislative intent and practical​
T
​realities, supporting large-load business development in Texas while still protecting grid​
 ​reliability and ratepayers. Our detailed comments below elaborate on each recommendation,​
  ​citing the specific draft rule subsections for reference.​


​ . ERCOT’s Share of the Large Load Study Fee (Draft​
1
​§25.194(c)(7))​
I​ssue:​
 ​The draft rule requires large load interconnection customers to pay a substantial study fee to​
  ​cover the costs of transmission studies by the interconnecting utility and ERCOT. However, as​
   ​currently structured, the majority of this fee goes to the utility, with only a relatively small portion​
 ​ llotted to ERCOT’s own study costs. For example, proposed subsection (c)(7)(A) sets a​
a
​minimum $114,000 study fee for a 75–250 MW load, which appears to include only ERCOT’s​
 ​base fee of about $14,000 (the Large Load Interconnection Study fee) and the rest for the​
  ​utility’s studies (​​epeconsulting.com​​). For larger loads (≥250 MW), the draft requires at least​
   ​$314,000, again implying that $300,000 would go to the utility and only $14,000 to ERCOT.​
    ​While the rule allows the fee to increase if study costs are higher, the base allocation to ERCOT​
     ​is minimal. Subsection (c)(7)(D) directs the utility to remit ERCOT’s portion of the fee to ERCOT,​
      ​but that portion is not explicitly stated and is evidently small.*​

​ ecommendation:​
R
​TBC recommends that the Commission increase the share of the study fee allocated to ERCOT.​
 ​This could entail raising the total study fee or adjusting the fee split so that ERCOT receives a​
  ​larger portion of the payment for each study. Ensuring ERCOT is properly compensated for its​
   ​role is critical because ERCOT’s analysis and oversight are indispensable to maintain system​
    ​reliability as large loads come online. ERCOT’s planning staff must review the utility’s study​
     ​results, run independent simulations if needed, and integrate large load forecasts into regional​
      ​planning models. The workload is significant – ERCOT has reviewed interconnection studies for​
       ​over 18,000 MW of large loads in the past two years (​​ercot.com​​), and the interconnection queue​
        ​continues to grow rapidly (​​ercot.com​​). Allocating a greater portion of the study fee to ERCOT​
         ​will provide resources for additional engineering staff, improved modeling tools, and faster​
          ​processing of large-load study approvals. This fee reallocation aligns with SB6’s directive to​
           ​facilitate business growth without compromising reliability (​​nrg.com​​). In practical terms, TBC​
            ​suggests the Commission consider setting a higher ERCOT fee component (for example, on the​
             ​order of tens of thousands of dollars more per study) or a percentage-based split that more​
              ​accurately reflects ERCOT’s effort. By strengthening ERCOT’s funding in subsection (c)(7), the​
               ​rule will help avoid study backlogs and ensure that large load projects—such as major data​
                ​centers and crypto mining facilities—are evaluated and interconnected expeditiously without​
                 ​shifting costs to other market participants.​

​ e also request commission to clarify that for the new power generation sites, the large load​
W
​fees are distinct from and not duplicative or generation interconnection study costs in order to​
 ​improve consistency and transparency.​

​ upport:​
S
​The draft rule already recognizes ERCOT’s role by requiring the utility to forward part of the​
 ​study fee to ERCOT. TBC’s proposal simply builds on this by adjusting the balance. We note​
  ​that $100,000 of the base fee is mandated by PURA §37.0561 to be paid to the utility​
   ​(​journals.senate.texas.gov​​); however, nothing in the statute prohibits setting a higher total fee or​
    ​directing a portion to ERCOT to cover its additional duties. Other regions have much higher​
     ​study deposits (sometimes refundable) for large loads (​​nrg.com​​), so the current Texas fee​
      ​structure can accommodate an increase if justified by workload. Given the unprecedented scale​
       ​of large load growth in ERCOT, providing ERCOT a larger share of the fee is both fair and​
        ​prudent. TBC believes this change will ultimately support faster interconnections and better​
         ​planning, benefiting both the industry and the ERCOT grid as a whole.​
 ​ . Limiting the $50,000/MW Financial Security to New Loads​
2
​(Draft §25.194(e)(8))​
I​ssue:​
 ​The draft rule imposes a financial security requirement of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak​
  ​demand for each large load customer. This requirement in proposed subsection (e)(8) is​
   ​intended as a deposit or security to ensure the customer’s financial commitment to the project,​
    ​guarding against cancellations that could leave unused transmission investments (“stranded​
     ​costs”). While TBC understands the rationale for requiring substantial security for new large​
      ​loads, we are concerned that the rule does not differentiate between entirely new​
       ​interconnection projects and expansions at existing sites. Under the current language, any​
        ​increase in contracted peak demand at a site ≥75 MW would trigger the $50k/MW security on​
         ​the full demand. This could penalize large load customers who expand an existing operation or​
          ​add load in phases, effectively treating a small expansion the same as a brand-new 100 MW​
           ​project. For example, an operational data center that initially contracted for 100 MW and later​
            ​adds 50 MW of load could be required to post $7.5 million in new security (assuming 150 MW​
             ​total), even though it already demonstrated viability and invested heavily in the first 100 MW​
              ​phase.​

​ ecommendation:​
R
​TBC urges the Commission to apply the $50,000/MW security requirement only to new​
 ​greenfield large load interconnections, or at least exclude incremental expansions at existing​
  ​sites from this full security payment. In practice, this could mean that once a large load​
   ​customer has established service at a site and satisfied the initial security for the originally​
    ​contracted capacity, any further expansion at that same site would either require no additional​
     ​security or a significantly reduced security proportional only to any new transmission upgrades​
      ​needed. The rule should make clear that “contracted peak demand” for purposes of subsection​
       ​(e)(8) refers to the demand of a new interconnection request, not a cumulative total that​
        ​penalizes growth. By limiting the scope to new projects, the Commission will encourage large​
         ​load customers to expand in Texas over time (adding jobs and investment) without facing​
          ​repetitive, outsized financial hurdles for each additional increment of load.​

​ upport:​
S
​Expansions at existing large-load facilities do not carry the same risk profile as brand-new​
 ​projects. An existing site has already demonstrated substantial commitment – it likely has​
  ​energized load, built infrastructure, and perhaps an operating track record. The risk of such a​
   ​customer abandoning an expansion midway is lower, meaning the need for a hefty security​
    ​deposit to backstop potential stranded grid upgrades is also lower. Moreover, many large​
     ​industrial and computing loads plan to grow in phases, as acknowledged by the rule’s​
      ​requirement for a phased energization schedule disclosure. If each phase is subject to an​
       ​additive $50k/MW security, the total financial burden can become prohibitive and may​
        ​discourage completing multi-phase projects. This runs counter to the legislative intent to​
         ​“support business development” for large loads in Texas (​​nrg.com​​). From a grid standpoint,​
          ​expansions at an existing site often leverage some pre-existing capacity or shared​
 i​nfrastructure, reducing the incremental strain on the system. It would be reasonable to calibrate​
 ​the security requirement to the actual new investment risk. For instance, the Commission could​
  ​specify that the $50k/MW applies only to the first interconnection agreement at a site (i.e. new​
   ​sites), and any subsequent load increases at that same site would either be exempt or require a​
    ​smaller supplemental security based on any new transmission facilities required. This approach​
     ​would still satisfy PURA §37.0561’s mandate for financial commitment to avoid stranded costs,​
      ​while not over-burdening established operations that are expanding. TBC notes that the draft​
       ​rule already provides flexibility in acceptable security forms (cash, parental guaranty, letter of​
        ​credit), which is helpful. Exempting or relaxing the requirement for expansions would be another​
         ​prudent refinement to ensure the rule targets the true risk (entirely new large loads) and not​
          ​deter healthy growth of existing large load sites.​


​3. Clarity on Release of Financial Security​
I​ssue:​
 ​The Staff Discussion Draft for Project No. 58481 establishes multiple requirements for large load​
  ​customers to post financial security or collateral to interconnecting electric utilities, including​
   ​per-megawatt security, security for long-lead equipment or services, and contributions in aid of​
    ​construction. The draft rule is detailed and prescriptive with respect to when and how such​
     ​financial security must be posted, but it does not provide equivalent clarity or consistency​
      ​regarding when that security will be released or refunded. Although the rule contains refund​
       ​provisions in certain enumerated circumstances—most notably in the event of a formal​
        ​withdrawal under subsection (i), capacity reallocation under subsection (j), or sustained​
         ​post-energization operations under subsection (k)—it does not establish a general principle or​
          ​uniform framework governing the return of security when underlying risks no longer exist.​

​ s drafted, the rule is largely silent on refund timing in several common and consequential​
A
​scenarios, including when ERCOT requires additional studies that materially alter or delay a​
 ​project, when interconnection assumptions change such that procurement or construction does​
  ​not proceed, when a customer elects not to move forward with a project outside of a formal​
   ​withdrawal under subsection (i), or when the interconnecting electric utility does not ultimately​
    ​incur the costs that the posted security was intended to cover and no explicit refund trigger​
     ​applies. In addition, the rule does not consistently pair each instance in which financial security​
      ​is required with a corresponding mechanism or timeline for its release. This creates uncertainty​
       ​for large load customers regarding how long substantial amounts of capital may remain​
        ​encumbered, even in circumstances where system reliability risks or stranded-cost concerns​
         ​have materially diminished.​

​ ecommendation:​
R
​The Commission should revise §25.194 to establish a clear, consistent, and comprehensive​
 ​framework governing the release and refund of financial security posted by large load​
  ​customers. At each point in the rule where financial security is required, whether for​
   ​per-megawatt security, long-lead equipment or services, or other pre-construction commitments,​
    ​the rule should include a corresponding mechanism and timeline for the return of that security​
 ​ hen the underlying cost or reliability risk no longer exists. Refund provisions should not be​
w
​limited solely to enumerated events such as formal withdrawal, capacity reallocation, or​
 ​post-energization milestones, but should instead reflect a general principle that unused or​
  ​unnecessary security must be returned within a defined period after it is determined that the​
   ​interconnecting electric utility will not incur the costs the security was intended to cover.​

​ pecifically, the Commission should clarify that financial security must be refunded when a​
S
​project is materially delayed, altered, or discontinued as a result of ERCOT study outcomes,​
 ​additional study requirements, or changes to interconnection assumptions that eliminate or​
  ​substantially reduce anticipated utility expenditures. The rule should also provide explicit refund​
   ​timelines for security posted for long-lead time equipment or services under subsection (h)(8) if​
    ​procurement does not occur or is no longer required. In addition, the Commission should clarify​
     ​the treatment of security when a customer elects not to proceed with a project outside of a​
      ​formal withdrawal under subsection (i), to ensure that customers are not required to maintain​
       ​posted security indefinitely in the absence of ongoing risk. We also recommend greater clarity​
        ​as to what entity determines when customer milestones are achieved.​

(​ k)(2) states load to sustain operations for 5 years to get the remaining refund. We propose the​
 ​following: Financial securities should be refunded once the risk of non-performance is mitigated​
  ​which is at energization or when the transmission infrastructure is put in service.​


​4. Reportable Changes​
I​ssue:​
 ​Subsection (d)(1) requires that "within 5 days of change, information disclosed in subsection (c)"​
  ​must be reported. The rule lacks clarity on what constitutes a reportable "change."​​Within a​
   ​dynamic model, a cable is considered an "electrical component." Given the range of​
    ​manufacturers and variability in cable length, which may not be finalized until installation,​
     ​planned cable lengths are subject to change during development.​

​ uring the development phase, many parameters evolve naturally. However, not all changes​
D
​affect load interconnection studies or reliability analyses. Requiring reporting of every minor​
 ​adjustment would impose an undue burden on both utilities and customers without providing​
  ​meaningful benefit to system reliability or planning.​

​ ecommendation:​
R
​Add clear guidance to subsection (d)(1) to define which types of changes must be reported,​
 ​specifically, those​​materially affecting system reliability or interconnection outcomes​​.​
  ​Minor technical adjustments that do not impact reliability analyses should be exempt.​​Provide​
   ​clarification that changes to disclosed information in subsection (c)​​do not impact the queue​
    ​position​​of a large load interconnection request.​​Customers need assurance that good-faith​
     ​updates to evolving technical details will not result in loss of queue priority.​
 I​ssue:​
 ​Subesction (e), the discretionary services requirement states: "Before the interconnecting​
  ​electric utility submits the large load interconnection study to ERCOT, the large load customer​
   ​must execute a discretionary services agreement that, at a minimum, includes the updated​
    ​disclosures and financial commitments under this subsection."​

​ ecommendation:​
R
​Remove this requirement as it is redundant because the same information is already provided​
 ​as part of the interconnection request approximately 30 days earlier. This additional step creates​
  ​unnecessary administrative burden for both customers and utilities without delivering added​
   ​value.​

I​ssue:​
 ​For Subsection (e)(5), the provision requires: "A large load customer must submit to the​
  ​interconnecting electric utility the large load customer's plans, expected timing, and current​
   ​progress for obtaining state and local regulatory approvals required for development before​
    ​energization (e.g., water, air, or backup generation permits, or city or county building permits)."​

​ ecommendation:​
R
​Remove the requirement to provide regulatory approvals at the interconnection study stage.​
 ​SB6 does not mandate this, and such approvals typically do not exist at this point in the​
  ​development process. Developers only pursue these permits after confirming when a site can​
   ​be energized, so requiring them earlier adds no value to ERCOT or TSP studies. This​
    ​requirement creates undue administrative burden without improving outcomes.​

I​ssue:​
 ​For Subection (g)(3). It states: "The interconnecting electric utility must provide a large load​
  ​customer timely information related to communications that the interconnecting electric utility​
   ​receives from ERCOT about the large load customer's interconnection request." The term​
    ​"timely" is undefined and subjective.​

​ ecommendation:​
R
​Given the strict energization and ramp-up schedule requirements for large load customers,​
 ​communication delays can significantly impact project timelines. To ensure transparency and​
  ​predictability, require utilities to notify customers​​within five (5) business days​​of receiving any​
   ​communication from ERCOT related to the customer's interconnection request. This​
    ​requirement would help customers adjust planning and business decisions promptly, reducing​
     ​the risk of delays to energization and ramp schedules.​

I​ssue:​
 ​The Intermediate Agreement provisions are overly broad and include duplicative requirements.​

​ ecommendation:​
R
​The Intermediate Agreement should serve a narrow and well-defined purpose: marking the​
 ​transition from transmission planning to construction by requiring enforceable financial and​
 ​ lectrical commitments. It should not function as a general development-status checkpoint or as​
e
​a repository for information that is duplicative, non-electrical, or inherently dynamic.​

​ hen structured properly, §25.194(h) can provide clarity, discipline, and protection against​
W
​stranded investment while remaining compatible with ERCOT's evolving planning frameworks,​
 ​including LIOO and future cluster studies.​

I​ssue:​
 ​The rule does not provide for appropriate crediting of study fees toward financial security​
  ​obligations.​

​ ecommendation​
R
​We understand and support SB6's policy objective of ensuring large loads pay their fair share of​
 ​transmission costs. SB6 states that any unused portion of the initial transmission screening​
  ​study fee should be applied as a credit toward financial obligations for procurement or​
   ​interconnection agreements at the same geographic site.​

​Therefore, the outstanding balance from the study fee should first be credited toward:​

   ​ .​ ​The $50,000/MW financial security fee​
   1
   ​2.​ ​The significant equipment or services costs​

​ ecurities posted under (h)(8) should be counted toward the Contribution in Aid of Construction​
S
​(CIAC) for equipment or services that fall under the items specified in the CIAC cost​
 ​contribution.​

I​ssue:​
 ​The rule does not adequately address refunds when capacity is reallocated or equipment is​
  ​reused.​

​ ecommendation:​
R
​In cases where equipment or services cannot be canceled, a load customer should receive a​
 ​refund if any ordered equipment, construction, or services are reused or deployed elsewhere in​
  ​the system. These assets continue to support the grid and do not create additional costs for​
   ​customers.​

​ ikewise, if transmission capacity freed by a withdrawal or reduction is immediately or​
L
​near-immediately utilized by other loads, there is no stranded investment. When another load​
 ​takes its place and transmission capacity remains fully utilized—or planned upgrades are still​
  ​needed to serve other interconnecting loads—no cost should be allocated to the withdrawing​
   ​project.​

I​ssue:​
 ​Subsection (l)(2) requires large loads to comply with unspecified operational standards. Without​
  ​clearly defined standards and robust stakeholder engagement, such a requirement is inherently​
   ​subjective and problematic.​
 ​ ecommendation:​
R
​Remove this language entirely. Large loads should not be obligated to meet undefined​
 ​operational criteria that may be impractical or impossible to achieve. Instead, focus on​
  ​collaborative efforts between ERCOT and stakeholders to develop​​market-based solutions​
   ​and​​well-defined operating standards​​that ensure system​​reliability through transparent​
    ​processes.​

​ xample:​
E
​Addressing issues such as Low Voltage Ride Through (LVRT) typically requires a combination​
 ​of measures, including:​

   ​​ L
   ●      ​ oad performance requirements​
   ​●​ ​Installation of devices​
    ​●​ ​Transmission system upgrades (e.g., improved spinning reserves or other system-wide​
          ​investments)​
     ​●​ ​Coordinated strategies from ERCOT​

​ osts for these solutions should be allocated based on a clear causation principle established​
C
​through the stakeholder process.​

​ dditional Comments​
A
​Section (h)(9) should note that in the event FERC establishes a non-firm load category, costs​
 ​could not be considered to have been incurred directly attributable to interconnecting the large​
  ​load customer.​

​ dditionally, there should be a​​review board within ERCOT​​to review the interconnecting​
A
​electric utility's estimated CIAC. The proposed rule requiring large loads to pay all of the CIAC is​
 ​a departure from how CIACs are normally handled and warrants independent oversight to​
  ​ensure accuracy and fairness.​


​Conclusion​
​ BC respectfully requests that the Commission incorporate the above recommendations into​
T
​the final Large Load Interconnection Standards rule. We believe these changes will improve the​
 ​rule’s balance between reliability protection and economic development, thereby fulfilling the​
  ​purpose of SB6. We appreciate the Commission’s consideration of our comments. TBC and its​
   ​member companies stand ready to assist and provide any further information as needed.​

​Thank you for the opportunity to participate in this important rulemaking.​

​Respectfully submitted,​

​ ee Bratcher, President​
L
​Texas Blockchain Council​
 ​Sources:​

   ​1.​ ​NRG Energy, Inc. Comments on PUCT Staff Questions, Project No. 58481 (Oct. 10, 2025)​
         ​nrg.com​​nrg.com​​.​

   ​2.​ ​Staff Discussion Draft Rule, 16 TAC §25.194 (Project No. 58481).​

   ​3.​ ​ERCOT Monthly Operational Overview (May 2025), highlighting large load interconnection​
          ​volumes​​ercot.com​​ercot.com​​.​
    ​4.​ ​Electric Power Engineers (EPE) Summary of ERCOT Large Load Interconnection Process (Apr.​
           ​21, 2025)​​epeconsulting.com​​.​




​Executive Summary​
​Comments from the Texas Blockchain Council​

​ BC generally supports the adoption of standardized large load interconnection criteria, but we​
T
​have a few concerns with the current Staff Discussion Draft of §25.194. For clarity, we​
 ​summarize our recommendations here (as requested in the rulemaking notice):​

   ​●​ W ​ e recommend increasing ERCOT’s Share of the Study Fee: The draft rule’s study fee​
         ​for large load interconnection studies (proposed §25.194(c)(7)) should allocate a larger​
          ​portion of the fee to ERCOT. As written, the minimum study fee is $114,000 for a 75–250​
           ​MW load and $314,000 for ≥250 MW, but only a small fraction of this fee is designated​
            ​for ERCOT’s use. TBC recommends increasing ERCOT’s share of the study fee to​
             ​ensure ERCOT is adequately funded to perform its critical system reliability analyses in​
              ​a timely manner.​
    ​●​ ​Limit the $50,000/MW Security to New Sites: The proposed financial security​
               ​requirement of $50,000 per MW (proposed §25.194(e)(8)) should apply only to​
                ​brand-new large load projects, not to incremental expansions at existing sites. The​
                 ​exception being an increase of 75 MWs or multiple increases that added up to 75 MWs​
                  ​to an existing site. TBC urges the Commission to exempt expansions (phased​
                   ​build-outs) at an existing large load facility from this hefty per-megawatt security deposit,​
                    ​as such expansions have already demonstrated substantial commitment and pose lower​
                     ​risk of abandonment compared to new greenfield projects. If ERCOT rejects or​
       ​ ubstantially modifies the interconnection application, that money should be refunded​
      s
      ​within 90 days. Specifically, section (4) on page 16 should include a sentence that​
       ​ensures a refund of the initial deposit if the interconnection proposal is not continued due​
        ​to additional study requirements from ERCOT.​
​●​      ​Section (h) (8) on pages 19 and 20 should include a timeline for the repayment of long​
          ​lead time electrical equipment security that was paid from the load to the interconnecting​
           ​electric utility.​
​●​         ​Section (h) (9) on page 20 should note that, in the event that FERC establishes a​
             ​non-firm load category, could not be considered to have incurred any costs directly​
              ​attributable to interconnecting the large load customer. In this section there should also​
               ​be a review board within ERCOT to review the interconnecting electric utility’s estimated​
                ​CIAC estimate since the proposed rule of having the large load pay all of the CIAC is a​
                 ​departure from how CIACs are normally handled.​
​●​               ​Section (k) (2) on page 24 should provide for repayment of security at the two year mark​
                   ​of sustained operations at peak demand period rather than a five year period or financial​
                    ​security should be refunded once the risk of non-performance is mitigated which is at​
                     ​energization or when the transmission infrastructure is put in service.​
​●​                   ​Section (L) (2) on page 24 requires large loads to comply with unspecified operational​
                       ​standards. Without clearly defined criteria and thorough stakeholder engagement, such​
                        ​a requirement is inherently subjective and could create significant challenges. Large​
                         ​loads should not be obligated to meet undefined operational expectations that may be​
                          ​impractical or unattainable. Therefore, TBC recommends removing this language and​
                           ​instead prioritizing the development of transparent, market-based solutions and​
                            ​well-defined operating standards for large loads to ensure system reliability.​

Dear Commissioners:

The Texas Blockchain Council (TBC) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the
proposed new 16 TAC §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards (Project No.
58481). TBC is an industry association representing Bitcoin mining and artificial intelligence (AI)
data center companies in Texas. Our members are among the "large load" customers that will
be directly affected by the new interconnection standards. We support the Commission's efforts
to implement Senate Bill 6 (codified as PURA §37.0561) to accommodate large loads in a
manner that "support[s] business development in this state while minimizing the potential for
stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability." In keeping with these goals,
TBC offers the following formal comments on the proposed rule.

These targeted modifications will better align the rule with legislative intent and practical
realities, supporting large-load business development in Texas while still protecting grid
reliability and ratepayers. Our detailed comments below elaborate on each recommendation,
citing the specific draft rule subsections for reference.


1. ERCOT's Share of the Large Load Study Fee (Draft
§25.194(c)(7))
Issue:
The draft rule requires large load interconnection customers to pay a substantial study fee to
cover the costs of transmission studies by the interconnecting utility and ERCOT. However, as
currently structured, the majority of this fee goes to the utility, with only a relatively small portion
 allotted to ERCOT's own study costs. For example, proposed subsection (c)(7)(A) sets a
minimum $114,000 study fee for a 75-250 MW load, which appears to include only ERCOT's
base fee of about $14,000 (the Large Load Interconnection Study fee) and the rest for the
utility's studies (epeconsulting.com). For larger loads (2250 MV\0, the draft requires at least
$314,000, again implying that $300,000 would go to the utility and only $14,000 to ERCOT.
While the rule allows the fee to increase if study costs are higher, the base allocation to ERCOT
is minimal. Subsection (c)(7)(D) directs the utility to remit ERCOT's portion of the fee to ERCOT,
but that portion is not explicitly stated and is evidently small.*

Recommendation:
TBC recommends that the Commission increase the share of the study fee allocated to ERCOT.
This could entail raising the total study fee or adjusting the fee split so that ERCOT receives a
larger portion of the payment for each study. Ensuring ERCOT is properly compensated for its
role is critical because ERCOT's analysis and oversight are indispensable to maintain system
reliability as large loads come online. ERCOT's planning staff must review the utility's study
results, run independent simulations if needed, and integrate large load forecasts into regional
planning models. The workload is significant - ERCOT has reviewed interconnection studies for
over 18,000 MW of large loads in the past two years (ercot.com), and the interconnection queue
continues to grow rapidly (ercot.com). Allocating a greater portion of the study fee to ERCOT
will provide resources for additional engineering staff, improved modeling tools, and faster
processing of large-load study approvals. This fee reallocation aligns with SB6's directive to
facilitate business growth without compromising reliability (nrq.com). In practical terms, TBC
suggests the Commission consider setting a higher ERCOT fee component (for example, on the
order of tens of thousands of dollars more per study) or a percentage-based split that more
accurately reflects ERCOT's effort. By strengthening ERCOT's funding in subsection (c)(7), the
rule will help avoid study backlogs and ensure that large load projects-such as major data
centers and crypto mining facilities-are evaluated and interconnected expeditiously without
shifting costs to other market participants.

We also request commission to clarify that for the new power generation sites, the large load
fees are distinct from and not duplicative or generation interconnection study costs in order to
improve consistency and transparency.

Support:
The draft rule already recognizes ERCOT's role by requiring the utility to forward part of the
study fee to ERCOT. TBC's proposal simply builds on this by adjusting the balance. We note
that $100,000 of the base fee is mandated by PURA §37.0561 to be paid to the utility
Oournals.senate.texas.gov); however, nothing in the statute prohibits setting a higher total fee or
directing a portion to ERCOT to cover its additional duties. Other regions have much higher
study deposits (sometimes refundable) for large loads (nrg.com), so the current Texas fee
structure can accommodate an increase if justified by workload. Given the unprecedented scale
of large load growth in ERCOT, providing ERCOT a larger share of the fee is both fair and
prudent. TBC believes this change will ultimately support faster interconnections and better
planning, benefiting both the industry and the ERCOT grid as a whole.
 2. Limiting the $50,000/MW Financial Security to New Loads
(Draft §25.194(e)(8))
Issue:
The draft rule imposes a financial security requirement of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak
demand for each large load customer. This requirement in proposed subsection (e)(8) is
intended as a deposit or security to ensure the customer's financial commitment to the project,
guarding against cancellations that could leave unused transmission investments ("stranded
costs"). While TBC understands the rationale for requiring substantial security for new large
loads, we are concerned that the rule does not differentiate between entirely new
interconnection projects and expansions at existing sites. Under the current language, any
increase in contracted peak demand at a site 275 MW would trigger the $50k/MW security on
the full demand. This could penalize large load customers who expand an existing operation or
add load in phases, effectively treating a small expansion the same as a brand-new 100 MW
project. For example, an operational data center that initially contracted for 100 MW and later
adds 50 MW of load could be required to post $7.5 million in new security (assuming 150 MW
total), even though it already demonstrated viability and invested heavily in the first 100 MW
phase.
Recommendation:
TBC urges the Commission to apply the $50,000/MW security requirement only to new
greenfield large load interconnections, or at least exclude incremental expansions at existing
sites from this full security payment. In practice, this could mean that once a large load
customer has established service at a site and satisfied the initial security for the originally
contracted capacity, any further expansion at that same site would either require no additional
security or a significantly reduced security proportional only to any new transmission upgrades
needed. The rule should make clear that "contracted peak demand" for purposes of subsection
(e)(8) refers to the demand of a new interconnection request, not a cumulative total that
penalizes growth. By limiting the scope to new projects, the Commission will encourage large
load customers to expand in Texas over time (adding jobs and investment) without facing
repetitive, outsized financial hurdles for each additional increment of load.

Support:
Expansions at existing large-load facilities do not carry the same risk profile as brand-new
projects. An existing site has already demonstrated substantial commitment - it likely has
energized load, built infrastructure, and perhaps an operating track record. The risk of such a
customer abandoning an expansion midway is lower, meaning the need for a hefty security
deposit to backstop potential stranded grid upgrades is also lower. Moreover, many large
industrial and computing loads plan to grow in phases, as acknowledged by the rule's
requirement for a phased energization schedule disclosure. If each phase is subject to an
additive $50k/MW security, the total financial burden can become prohibitive and may
discourage completing multi-phase projects. This runs counter to the legislative intent to
"support business development" for large loads in Texas (nrg.com). From a grid standpoint,
expansions at an existing site often leverage some pre-existing capacity or shared
 infrastructure, reducing the incremental strain on the system. It would be reasonable to calibrate
the security requirement to the actual new investment risk. For instance, the Commission could
specify that the $50k/MW applies only to the first interconnection agreement at a site (i.e. new
sites), and any subsequent load increases at that same site would either be exempt or require a
smaller supplemental security based on any new transmission facilities required. This approach
would still satisfy PURA §37.0561's mandate for financial commitment to avoid stranded costs,
while not over-burdening established operations that are expanding. TBC notes that the draft
rule already provides flexibility in acceptable security forms (cash, parental guaranty, letter of
credit), which is helpful. Exempting or relaxing the requirement for expansions would be another
prudent refinement to ensure the rule targets the true risk (entirely new large loads) and not
deter healthy growth of existing large load sites.


3. Clarity on Release of Financial Security
Issue:
The Staff Discussion Draft for Project No. 58481 establishes multiple requirements for large load
customers to post financial security or collateral to interconnecting electric utilities, including
per-megawatt security, security for long-lead equipment or services, and contributions in aid of
construction. The draft rule is detailed and prescriptive with respect to when and how such
financial security must be posted, but it does not provide equivalent clarity or consistency
regarding when that security will be released or refunded. Although the rule contains refund
provisions in certain enumerated circumstances-most notably in the event of a formal
withdrawal under subsection (i), capacity reallocation under subsection (j), or sustained
post-energization operations under subsection (k)-it does not establish a general principle or
uniform framework governing the return of security when underlying risks no longer exist.

As drafted, the rule is largely silent on refund timing in several common and consequential
scenarios, including when ERCOT requires additional studies that materially alter or delay a
project, when interconnection assumptions change such that procurement or construction does
not proceed, when a customer elects not to move forward with a project outside of a formal
withdrawal under subsection (i), or when the interconnecting electric utility does not ultimately
incur the costs that the posted security was intended to cover and no explicit refund trigger
applies. In addition, the rule does not consistently pair each instance in which financial security
is required with a corresponding mechanism or timeline for its release. This creates uncertainty
for large load customers regarding how long substantial amounts of capital may remain
encumbered, even in circumstances where system reliability risks or stranded-cost concerns
have materially diminished.

Recommendation:
The Commission should revise §25.194 to establish a clear, consistent, and comprehensive
framework governing the release and refund of financial security posted by large load
customers. At each point in the rule where financial security is required, whether for
per-megawatt security, long-lead equipment or services, or other pre-construction commitments,
the rule should include a corresponding mechanism and timeline for the return of that security
 when the underlying cost or reliability risk no longer exists. Refund provisions should not be
limited solely to enumerated events such as formal withdrawal, capacity reallocation, or
post-energization milestones, but should instead reflect a general principle that unused or
unnecessary security must be returned within a defined period after it is determined that the
interconnecting electric utility will not incur the costs the security was intended to cover.

Specifically, the Commission should clarify that financial security must be refunded when a
project is materially delayed, altered, or discontinued as a result of ERCOT study outcomes,
additional study requirements, or changes to interconnection assumptions that eliminate or
substantially reduce anticipated utility expenditures. The rule should also provide explicit refund
timelines for security posted for long-lead time equipment or services under subsection (h)(8) if
procurement does not occur or is no longer required. In addition, the Commission should clarify
the treatment of security when a customer elects not to proceed with a project outside of a
formal withdrawal under subsection (i), to ensure that customers are not required to maintain
posted security indefinitely in the absence of ongoing risk. We also recommend greater clarity
as to what entity determines when customer milestones are achieved.

(k)(2) states load to sustain operations for 5 years to get the remaining refund. We propose the
following: Financial securities should be refunded once the risk of non-performance is mitigated
which is at energization or when the transmission infrastructure is put in service.

4. Reportable Changes
Issue:
Subsection (d)(1) requires that "within 5 days of change, information disclosed in subsection (c)"
must be reported. The rule lacks clarity on what constitutes a reportable "change." Within a
dynamic model, a cable is considered an "electrical component." Given the range of
manufacturers and variability in cable length, which may not be finalized until installation,
planned cable lengths are subject to change during development.

During the development phase, many parameters evolve naturally. However, not all changes
affect load interconnection studies or reliability analyses. Requiring reporting of every minor
adjustment would impose an undue burden on both utilities and customers without providing
meaningful benefit to system reliability or planning.

Recommendation:
Add clear guidance to subsection (d)(1) to define which types of changes must be reported,
specifically, those materially affecting system reliability or interconnection outcomes.
Minor technical adjustments that do not impact reliability analyses should be exempt. Provide
clarification that changes to disclosed information in subsection (c) do not impact the queue
position of a large load interconnection request. Customers need assurance that good-faith
updates to evolving technical details will not result in loss of queue priority.
 Issue:
Subesction (e), the discretionary services requirement states: "Before the interconnecting
electric utility submits the large load interconnection study to ERCOT, the large load customer
must execute a discretionary services agreement that, at a minimum, includes the updated
disclosures and financial commitments under this subsection."

Recommendation:
Remove this requirement as it is redundant because the same information is already provided
as part of the interconnection request approximately 30 days earlier. This additional step creates
unnecessary administrative burden for both customers and utilities without delivering added
value.

Issue:
For Subsection (e)(5), the provision requires: "A large load customer must submit to the
interconnecting electric utility the large load customer's plans, expected timing, and current
progress for obtaining state and local regulatory approvals required for development before
energization (e.g., water, air, or backup generation permits, or city or county building permits)."

Recommendation:
Remove the requirement to provide regulatory approvals at the interconnection study stage.
SB6 does not mandate this, and such approvals typically do not exist at this point in the
development process. Developers only pursue these permits after confirming when a site can
be energized, so requiring them earlier adds no value to ERCOT or TSP studies. This
requirement creates undue administrative burden without improving outcomes.

Issue:
For Subection (g)(3). It states: "The interconnecting electric utility must provide a large load
customer timely information related to communications that the interconnecting electric utility
receives from ERCOT about the large load customer's interconnection request." The term
"timely" is undefined and subjective.

Recommendation:
Given the strict energization and ramp-up schedule requirements for large load customers,
communication delays can significantly impact project timelines. To ensure transparency and
predictability, require utilities to notify customers within five (5) business days of receiving any
communication from ERCOT related to the customer's interconnection request. This
requirement would help customers adjust planning and business decisions promptly, reducing
the risk of delays to energization and ramp schedules.

Issue:
The Intermediate Agreement provisions are overly broad and include duplicative requirements.

Recommendation:
The Intermediate Agreement should serve a narrow and well-defined purpose: marking the
transition from transmission planning to construction by requiring enforceable financial and
 electrical commitments. It should not function as a general development-status checkpoint or as
a repository for information that is duplicative, non-electrical, or inherently dynamic.

When structured properly, §25.194(h) can provide clarity, discipline, and protection against
stranded investment while remaining compatible with ERCOT's evolving planning frameworks,
including LIOO and future cluster studies.

Issue:
The rule does not provide for appropriate crediting of study fees toward financial security
obligations.

Recommendation
We understand and support SB6's policy objective of ensuring large loads pay their fair share of
transmission costs. SB6 states that any unused portion of the initial transmission screening
study fee should be applied as a credit toward financial obligations for procurement or
interconnection agreements at the same geographic site.

Therefore, the outstanding balance from the study fee should first be credited toward:

   1. The $50,000/MW financial security fee
   2. The significant equipment or services costs

Securities posted under (h)(8) should be counted toward the Contribution in Aid of Construction
(CIAC) for equipment or services that fall under the items specified in the CIAC cost
contribution.

Issue:
The rule does not adequately address refunds when capacity is reallocated or equipment is
reused.

Recommendation:
In cases where equipment or services cannot be canceled, a load customer should receive a
refund if any ordered equipment, construction, or services are reused or deployed elsewhere in
the system. These assets continue to support the grid and do not create additional costs for
customers.

Likewise, if transmission capacity freed by a withdrawal or reduction is immediately or
near-immediately utilized by other loads, there is no stranded investment. When another load
takes its place and transmission capacity remains fully utilized-or planned upgrades are still
needed to serve other interconnecting loads-no cost should be allocated to the withdrawing
project.

Issue:
Subsection (I)(2) requires large loads to comply with unspecified operational standards. Without
clearly defined standards and robust stakeholder engagement, such a requirement is inherently
subjective and problematic.
 Recommendation:
Remove this language entirely. Large loads should not be obligated to meet undefined
operational criteria that may be impractical or impossible to achieve. Instead, focus on
collaborative efforts between ERCOT and stakeholders to develop market-based solutions
and well-defined operating standards that ensure system reliability through transparent
processes.
Example:
Addressing issues such as Low Voltage Ride Through (LVRT) typically requires a combination
of measures, including:

    •   Load performance requirements
    •   Installation of devices
    •   Transmission system upgrades (e.g., improved spinning reserves or other system-wide
        investments)
    •   Coordinated strategies from ERCOT

Costs for these solutions should be allocated based on a clear causation principle established
through the stakeholder process.

Additional Comments
Section (h)(9) should note that in the event FERC establishes a non-firm load category, costs
could not be considered to have been incurred directly attributable to interconnecting the large
load customer.

Additionally, there should be a review board within ERCOT to review the interconnecting
electric utility's estimated CIAC. The proposed rule requiring large loads to pay all of the CIAC is
a departure from how CIACs are normally handled and warrants independent oversight to
ensure accuracy and fairness.


Conclusion
TBC respectfully requests that the Commission incorporate the above recommendations into
the final Large Load Interconnection Standards rule. We believe these changes will improve the
rule's balance between reliability protection and economic development, thereby fulfilling the
purpose of SB6. We appreciate the Commission's consideration of our comments. TBC and its
member companies stand ready to assist and provide any further information as needed.

Thank you for the opportunity to participate in this important rulemaking.

Respectfully submitted,

Lee Bratcher, President
